# PREFACE

The mystical movement in Judaism is among the oldest subjects in the study of religion. It has been viewed from the most diverse perspectives for more than 400 years, and all the shifts of the ages are reflected in the extraordinarily varied evaluations and descriptions it has received. It has been met with every possible emotion, ranging from every nuance of recognition and delight to the most bitter, even contemptuous, rejection. The passion of these positions—especially on the part of Jewish critics of this movement—proves how often this was not a matter of researching deep-seated scientific facts, but rather a matter of polemics and a confrontation with a historical power still active in the present. Indeed, the abundance of works dedicated specifically to the *Kabbalah* <note>The primary system of Jewish esoteric mysticism.</note> stands in no proportion to the depth of insight that might reasonably be expected from such long and steady engagement with these phenomena. 

The almost unanimous rejection expressed by the classic representatives of Jewish scholarship in their statements on the Kabbalah and its branches—a rejection that, in the case of Heinrich Grätz <note>1817–1891; a foundational historian of Judaism known for his rationalist bias against mysticism.</note>, the most famous historian of the Jewish people, intensified into fanatical blindness—represents less the scientific judgment of a generation of rationalists than a naturally one-sided struggle against a power still perceived as present. Scholarship did not encounter this power with the love of understanding or on its own level, but rather in the armor of an opponent and on the level of a great historical conflict. To us of the later generations, the polemical weapons of this scholarship all too often appear dull. Only the general transformation of the 19th century...

<summary>The author introduces the history of Kabbalah scholarship, arguing that past Jewish historians (like Heinrich Grätz) were too biased by rationalism and contemporary polemics to objectively study Jewish mysticism.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Jewish Mysticism, Historiography, Heinrich Grätz, Rationalism, Religious Studies</keywords>

# PREFACE

The dominant ideas in the history of religion have shifted, coinciding with profound changes within Judaism itself. These shifts have opened the path toward an unbiased view of the nature and significance of Jewish mysticism. Such a view will no longer be opened from a Christian perspective—as was the case with almost all older works, which were often profound—nor from the perspective of a polemic, no matter how historically justified it might be. Instead, it will arise from a living but sober understanding of the subject itself and the internal laws governing it. Thus, research in this field stands today at a new beginning, facing a difficult but fruitful task.

In such a situation, bibliographic research takes on special importance. Today, at the start of a new period of research, almost no one has even an approximate overview of the literature in this field. No adequate bibliographic account has yet been given, either of the existing mystical sources and texts themselves or of the descriptive and analytical studies concerning them. Two tasks naturally present themselves, the solution of which could provide fundamental help to future researchers.

The first task—a bibliography of the actual mystical literature, the <term>Kabbalistic</term> <note>original: kabbalistischen; referring to the tradition of Jewish mysticism</note> and <term>Hasidic</term> <note>original: chassidischen; referring to the popular mystical movement arising in the 18th century</note> works themselves—cannot be undertaken in Western Europe today with any prospect of success. The number of Russian-Polish and Oriental <note>In this context, "Oriental" refers to Jewish communities in the Middle East and North Africa.</note> editions that are nowhere recorded and hardly to be found in public libraries is far too high, especially those from later periods. Their importance, particularly regarding <term>Hasidic literature</term>, is far too great for them to be neglected. Of the estimated 2,000 titles of specifically Kabbalistic literature and 3,000 titles of Hasidic literature, only a small portion can be identified in accessible collections.¹ This is especially true since no known library possesses true special collections in this field, which was so despised during the era of the classic book collectors. Consequently, the sheer volume of this literature, particularly regarding printed material, is usually significantly underestimated. Only many years of work in Eastern Europe or the Orient, combined with knowledge of the two great American collections in New York (Jewish Theological Seminary...

---

<note>¹ I base my estimate on several years of observation in Jerusalem, which is perhaps the place richest in works of this kind in the world.</note>

<keywords>Jewish mysticism, Kabbalah, Hasidism, bibliography, religious history, Jerusalem, New York, Jewish Theological Seminary</keywords>

<page-num>XI</page-num>

<header>->**PREFACE**<-</header>

Seminary) and Cincinnati (Hebrew Union College), might yield something useful. Thus, this bibliography of texts—which would also have to process the treasures of manuscripts that are so infinitely rich specifically in the field of mysticism—must remain a pressing <term>desideratum</term> <note>original: "Desideratum"; something desired but currently missing</note> of scholarship. The appendix of this book, containing the long-overdue and certainly widely desired bibliography of *Zohar* editions and commentaries, may serve as a specimen of such a bibliography of sources.

Under current circumstances, the second task is more feasible, and its solution is the goal of the present book: to provide as complete an account as possible of the literature on Jewish mysticism available in printed books and articles. This aims to provide researchers and collectors with an overview of what has been achieved in this field to date. It is a fact that most authors here have remained almost completely unaware of the achievements or failures of their predecessors. Important clarifications and materials, published in remote places, have been buried and never noticed. Long-corrected errors still pass from hand to hand because no one has read the correction. Indeed, the best-known general accounts, which are repeatedly copied, have become—for whatever reasons—the most dangerous sources of error and obstacles to advancing knowledge. 

It is a fact that among the abundance of those who have written about Jewish mysticism, only a vanishingly small number possessed a well-founded and authoritative knowledge of it. The tendency—even among Jewish scholars—to judge half-knowledge and unfounded assertions leniently is likely greater here than in any other field of religious history or Jewish studies. A blatant and glaring scandal of scholarship occurred at the beginning of this century: the French translation of the *Zohar* by Jean de Pauly. At the time, it did not call a single critic to the scene who would have examined even 25 pages in detail. Thus, a work based on ignorance and continuous, highly impudent forgeries could become the momentary main source of information for various circles, including the scientific community. This proves most clearly how defenseless the Kabbalah was left to amateurism. The proportion of such often extremely pretentious ignorance and half-knowledge in the literature recorded here is large. And yet, as is the case with all questions that cannot be answered exclusively from a philological <note>the study of language in oral and written historical sources</note> perspective, even in...

<meta>This page continues the author's introductory remarks regarding the methodology and scope of his bibliographical research into Jewish mysticism.</meta>

<page-num>XII</page-num>

->**PREFACE**<-

In such works, especially those originating from mystical circles, there is still much beneficial material to be discovered. The unbiased critic will find objective insight and depth in many strange works—even those that are completely flawed from a philological <note>original: *Philologischen*; the study of language in oral and written historical sources</note> perspective—provided they were conceived with intellectual honesty. Indeed, historical-philological intuition and objective-philosophical intuition have, for the most part, unfortunately drifted apart in Kabbalah research. Anyone who strives to understand spiritual connections, such as a researcher of mystical movements and doctrines, should not disdain any such source. One must be careful not to reject "unscientific" statements with that gesture of arrogance which contradicts the dignity of research. Furthermore, the boundaries between intellectual honesty and dishonest bluffing are, as far as I can judge, not difficult to draw among the works listed here.

To help understand the intent of this bibliography and its limits, I would like to offer the following preliminary remarks.

Included here are works specifically dealing with Talmudic mysticism and Jewish Gnosticism <note>original: *Gnosis*; a prominent philosophical and religious movement emphasizing secret knowledge</note>, as well as everything concerning the mystical movement from the post-Talmudic period to the present: Gaonic mysticism, the Kabbalah in the narrower sense (that is, the classical form of the movement as it recognizably emerged since the 12th century), the Messianic movements and sects of a mystical and mystical-antinomian <note>original: *antinomistischen*; the belief that under gospel dispensation, the moral law is of no use or obligation</note> character originating from it—such as Sabbatianism and Frankism—and Hasidism, which represents the final historical stage of this long development. Finally, I have included the magical and occult realms and disciplines of the so-called "Practical" Kabbalah, which represents the border province between mysticism and folklore. 

In individual cases, the boundaries were often difficult to draw; I have endeavored to decide doubtful cases based on the significance of the work in question for the knowledge of mysticism. For instance, the exact boundary between mystical and non-mystical material in Talmudic literature has yet to be determined and is currently quite controversial. Therefore, only works specifically dedicated to the subject are included here. The same difficulty applies to the very fluid boundaries between scholarly and popular magic. I have fundamentally excluded the extremely extensive literature on the Essenes <note>a Jewish sect during the Second Temple period</note>, except for those works in which the (true or alleged) relationships between Essenism and later Jewish mysticism and the Kabbalah are the subject of specific investigation. Especially regarding...

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<page-num>XIII</page-num>
->**PREFACE**<-

Regarding the literature on the Essenes <note>A Jewish sect during the Second Temple period</note>, there are already enough existing bibliographic references. Likewise, works specifically concerning the Biblical period are not included here, as I have not been able to convince myself that there was a mystical movement in Judaism during that period—let alone one connected to the 2,000-year historical continuity of Rabbinic Jewish mysticism treated in this work. For Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> and the apocalyptic movement, both of which also border the subject of this work, all necessary bibliographic work has already been performed by philologists and theologians. To increase the scope of this book infinitely by including such material, which is well-known elsewhere, would have meant making its publication practically impossible. The prehistory, appearance, and branches of the Kabbalah alone remain the subject of this bibliography.

I have excluded Hebrew biographies belonging to the mystical literature itself—such as those of Isaac Luria, Hayyim Vital, and the endless series of (often valuable) biographies of Hasidic *Zaddikim* <term>righteous leaders of Hasidic communities</term> written by their own followers—because they possess the character of primary sources. As previously stated, a bibliography of primary sources cannot be provided here. In borderline cases, I have decided in favor of inclusion. Furthermore, a considerable amount of material, particularly of a biographical nature, could likely still be identified in Yiddish periodical and newspaper literature, which is probably only fully accessible in Poland or America and has remained unknown to me.

Naturally, a bibliography of Jewish mysticism should not include writings that a closer examination shows to have the word "Kabbalah" or "Kabbalistic" in the title, but otherwise have nothing to do with the subject and are of no importance for the knowledge of Jewish mysticism. The number of such writings is large. I have become aware, directly or indirectly, of many German, English, French, Latin, and Polish books of this kind. In these cases, "Kabbalah" stands either as a symbolic designation for any kind of secret knowledge in general—as in a wealth of alchemical and occultist writings, such as "Kabbalah, Mirror of Art and Nature" <note>original: *Cabbala, speculum artis et naturae*</note> and the like¹—or for various other subjects that were labeled with the pseudonym of Kabbalah at different times and for different reasons, such as writings...

***

¹ A large number of such works are listed in Kopp (No. 672 of this bibliography) as well as in Caillet's *Bibliographic Manual of Psychic Sciences* <note>original: *Manuel bibliographique des sciences psychiques*</note>, though their material cannot claim any degree of completeness.

<page-num>XIV</page-num>
->**PREFACE**<-

...regarding the Lullian art <note>original: "lullische Kunst"; a logical and philosophical system developed by the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull, which later Christian scholars often associated with Kabbalah</note> or a number of 17th and 18th-century English and French writings that are purely political or state-theoretical in content—such as the well-known *Lettres Cabbalistiques* <note>Cabbalistic Letters; despite the title, this was a work of social and political satire by the Marquis d'Argens</note> and others. In doubtful cases where I could not conduct a personal examination <note>original: "Autopsie"</note> to reach a final decision, I opted for inclusion at the risk of being in error (as with entry No. 204).

With the supplements, this bibliography includes more than 1,300 entries and is likely still capable of many additions. About 500 to 600 of these entries exist as independent bibliographic units. A large number of these specific writings are difficult, if not impossible, to obtain; there is likely no public collection that possesses even half of them. It would be a welcome result of this bibliography if it served as an incentive for some collections to supplement their holdings. Twelve languages are represented in the works listed here, including almost all of the more important ones. To make them easier to navigate, I have also provided English <note>original: "deutsch" (German)</note> translations for Hebrew, Slavic, and Hungarian titles. The complete absence of Spanish (except for No. 867) and Scandinavian works is striking. Even experts in Jewish literature in these languages were unable to point out anything relevant to me. I am certain that a significant number of works I missed or that remained inaccessible to me still exist in other languages, particularly in English, Russian, and Yiddish periodicals. I will be grateful for any additions and corrections from experts aimed at addressing these deficiencies, of which I am painfully aware.

I have endeavored to provide the sources for my information to the best of my knowledge for all works that neither I nor reliable informants were able to see personally. Because the rich holdings of the Jewish National and University Library in Jerusalem <note>Now known as the National Library of Israel</note> were available to me for several years, I had the opportunity in many cases for a precise and repeated verification of information from other sources. My aim was to provide as accurate and detailed information as possible, particularly by providing the pagination and similar details to help the users of this bibliography identify incomplete or faulty copies...

---

¹ See, for example, Watt, *Bibliotheca Britannica* under the heading <note>original: "s. v." (sub voce)</note> "Cabala."

<page-num>XV</page-num>

<header>->**PREFACE**<-</header>

...in order to enable completeness checks. Almost all major Judaic bibliographies fail completely for such purposes, as every user knows from painful experience. Through the energetic support I have received from many sides, I was also able to obtain accurate and reliable information about many works that were not available in Jerusalem <note>Gershom Scholem moved to Jerusalem in 1923 to work at the National Library, which explains the geographic context of his research</note>. In individual cases, many additions are still possible and desirable through personal inspection <note>original: "Autopsie"; in bibliography, this refers to the physical examination of a book by the researcher</note>.

The previous research I was able to use was only practical and valuable where it concerned smaller sections of the overall field of Jewish mysticism. This applies to the information provided by Wolf in the *Hebrew Library* <note>original: *Bibliotheca Hebraea*; a monumental four-volume bibliography by Johann Christoph Wolf published 1715–1733</note> Volumes II and IV for the older period up to approximately 1725, which I have endeavored to complete and correct in many details. It also applies to the references by Schwab in his *Index of Articles* <note>original: *Répertoire des articles*; a reference work by Moïse Schwab indexing Jewish scholarly articles from the 19th century</note>, and above all, the very valuable references to Russian works—specifically regarding Hasidism <note>term: **Hasidism**; a Jewish spiritual and mystical movement that arose in 18th-century Eastern Europe</note>—which are given in the *Systematic Register of Literature about Jews in the Russian Language from 1708–1889* <note>original: *Sistemičeskij ukazatel literatury o Jevrejach*</note>, published as a supplement to the journal *The Sunrise* <note>original: *Woschod*</note>. Bibliographies in encyclopedia articles offered very little material, especially for more obscure literature.

For the specific purpose pursued here, the large bibliography by Caillet on the entire field of occultism offered extremely little that was useful. Even less was found in the completely useless, allegedly "only" special bibliography of the Kabbalah by Papus <note>original: Gérard Encausse, known as Papus (1865–1916), a famous French physician and occultist who popularized a version of Kabbalah that Scholem found historically inaccurate</note> (Entry No. 894). These two French occultists, like their entire school, associate the word *Kabbalah* <note>original: *Cabbale*</note> with such a broad meaning that the writings they label as Kabbalistic—journal articles are entirely missing here, as is the entire literature on Hasidism—deal with almost everything *except* Jewish mysticism. Where Maimonides <note>term: **Maimonides** (1138–1204); the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and rationalist. Scholem is mocking the occultists for labeling a rationalist philosopher as a "great Kabbalist"</note> is regarded as a "great Kabbalist" and the Mishnah and Talmud <note>term: **Mishnah and Talmud**; the foundational legal and theological texts of Rabbinic Judaism</note> are classified among Kabbalistic writings, little instruction can be hoped for or found in this area. All details in the work of Papus are, moreover, of grotesque inaccuracy and unreliability. Works written in Hebrew are completely missing in both authors' works.

Finally, the catalogs of second-hand bookstores—especially those of occultist bookshops—form a source of literature on the Kabbalah that is not without danger, but nonetheless indispensable. In many cases, they have been of significant use to me through indirect hints. These sources also generally excel in nothing less than reliability, particularly as a result of their consistent...

...the frequent mixing of all writings that carry the name Kabbalah <note>original: "Kabbala"; the Jewish mystical tradition</note> in their title in some way.

This bibliography was begun in 1919 using the resources of German libraries and was completed in 1925 in Jerusalem. Heartfelt thanks are expressed here to all those who contributed to the completion of this work through suggestions, remarks, comparisons, and corrections, especially to: Dr. D. Z. Baneth (Jerusalem); Dr. Rob. Eisler (Paris); Prof. A. Freimann (Frankfurt); Dr. W. Heilbrunn (Berlin); Prof. Alexander Marx (New York), who read the proofs for a large part of the book and provided me with very valuable additions for the supplement; Moses Marx (Berlin); Dr. Heinz Pflaum (Jerusalem); Js. Rivkind (New York); Dr. A. Spanier (Berlin); and Dr. A. Z. Schwarz (Vienna); as well as the library administrations in Gießen, Halle, and Rostock, who answered my inquiries most willingly. Dr. Hugo Bergmann (Jerusalem), Director of the Jewish National and University Library, supported my work in every possible way. I am also particularly indebted to the cooperation of the Drugulin publishing house <note>original: "Verlag Drugulin"; a prestigious German printing house in Leipzig famous for its high-quality scholarly typography</note>, which fulfilled my wishes in the most generous manner during the printing process and did everything possible to give the book a beautiful appearance.

Jerusalem, November 1926

G. S. <note>Gershom Scholem (1897–1982), a primary founder of the modern academic study of Jewish mysticism</note>

8 ABRAHAM OF WORMS [Pseudonym?] The Jew Abraham of Worms's *Book of True Practice in Ancient Divine Magic and in Amazing Things, as Communicated through the Holy Kabbalah and through Elohym <note>original: Elohym, a Hebrew name for God</note> . . . Cologne on the Rhine, Peter Hammer, 1725.
->[Reprints:] Stuttgart, Scheible [?], 1853. [Anastatic reprint <term>anastatic reprint: a facsimile reproduction produced through a chemical transfer process</term>.]<-

9 — *The Book of the Sacred Magic of Abra-Melin [!] the Mage, as delivered by Abraham the Jew unto his son Lamech A.D. 1458.* Translated from the original Hebrew into French and now rendered from the latter language into English. From a unique [!! see below!] and valuable manuscript in the “Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal” <note>original French: "Arsenal Library"</note> at Paris. By S. L. MacGregor Mathers.
->[First edition:] London, Luzac & Co., 1898. XLVIII, 268 pages. Octavo.<-
->Second edition, London, Luzac; New York, Theosophical Publishing Company, no date <note>original Latin: "s. a." (sine anno)</note>. XLVIII, 268 pages. Octavo.<-

[This is one of the most important internationally circulated magical texts. Its claim of Jewish origin does not seem far-fetched. The following manuscript versions have come to my attention: a Hebrew one in Oxford (Neubauer, Catalogue column 702) Code 2051 titled *The Book of the Treasure of Kings* <note>original Hebrew: "Sefer Segullat Melakhim"</note>; a German one in Vienna V No. 10580 [the number 89 in Steinschneider’s cited work is a typo], which is perhaps identical to the one mentioned by Kopp in *The History of Alchemy* <note>original German: "die Alchemie"</note> II, 236; an Italian one, V No. 10579; and a French one, which—in addition to the one mentioned by Mathers—is a manuscript listed by Papus in *The Kabbalah* <note>original French: "la Kabbale"</note> in Bibliography No. 49 (from the de Guaita library). The book possesses a thoroughly Jewish character. The manuscripts date back as far as the 16th century. Christian interpolations <term>interpolations: later additions or alterations to a text</term> are few. The two printed versions complement each other well. In general, the English-French version is superior. In that version, the magic words are always correctly written as magic squares <note>original German: "Zauberplaketten"</note>. Mathers’s notes and introduction—both very extensive—are not without value, but must be used with great caution. The English version is somewhat more "Christianized," yet it omits specifically those interpolations found in the German version—for example, the passage on page 104 of the Berlin printing concerning Jesus, his disciples, and the Apocalypse! The chronological dates differ between the versions. Mathers is unaware of the German printing. Steinschneider, in *Hebrew Translations* <note>original German: "Hebr. Übersetzungen"</note> § 543, considers the book a forgery by a Christian impostor; however, such an author would have possessed remarkably good knowledge of Hebrew for the 15th century (when it likely originated) and even for the 16th century—see the entire fourth book, especially in the English edition, where the names are even better preserved. Book 2 is entirely missing in that edition, which is why only three books are counted there. See also Wolf III, 67; IV, 757–59; Lehmann, *Superstition and Magic* <note>original German: "Aberglaube u. Zauberei"</note> 2nd edition 1908, page 251; and Scholem in *Monatsschrift für Geschichte und Wissenschaft des Judentums* <note>Monthly Journal for the History and Science of Judaism</note> 69, page 95.]

<summary>This page catalogs various editions and manuscripts of the "Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage," including the famous translation by S.L. MacGregor Mathers. The bibliographer argues for the text's authentic Jewish origins despite later Christian additions.</summary>

31 [ANONYMOUS]. *A Miscellaneous Metaphysical Essay, or an Hypothesis concerning the Formation and Generation of Spiritual and Material Beings, with their several Characteristics and Properties, and how far the several surrounding Beings partake of either property. To which is added some Thoughts upon Creation in General, upon Pre-existence, the Cabalistic Account of the Mosaic Creation, the Formation of Adam and Fall of Mankind and upon the Nature of Noah's Deluge. As also upon the Dormant State of the Soul, from the Creation to our Birth and from our Death to the Resurrection. The whole considered upon the Principles of Reason, and from the Tenor of the Revelations in the Holy Scriptures.* By an impartial Inquirer after Truth. London, no date <note>original Latin: *s. a.* (sine anno)</note> and without printer information.
[“An explanatory treatise on the Kabbalah,” see Hargrave Jennings, *The Rosicrucians*, German edition, Berlin 1912, Vol. II, pages 214–215, who had a copy. Judging by the title, it was written in the spirit of Henry More <note>Henry More (1614–1687) was a prominent Cambridge Platonist who sought to reconcile Christian theology with Kabbalistic and Platonic philosophy</note>.]

Warsaw 1844. 81 pages. Octavo (8°).

[Deals with the numerology <note>original German: *Zahlenlehre*</note> of the Kabbalah and the *Sefer Yetzirah* <note>original German: *Jezira*, the "Book of Formation," one of the earliest extant Jewish esoteric texts</note>. [“Documents of Brotherhood” — two important documents on the history of the mystical movement in Jerusalem around 1750, which had its center in Rabbi Shalom Mizrahi Shar’abi. By <term>hitkashrut</term> <note>association or binding</note> the Kabbalists understood the entering into a mystical communism of spiritual goods and suffering. Among the signatories are Jacob and Yom-Tob Algazi as well as Ch. J. D. Azulai. One of the documents was also printed by A. S. Rabbinowicz in 1923. Much regarding such <term>mikh-tevei hitkashrut</term> <note>letters of association</note> is also found in the book *Mareh Tovot* by Raphael Ohana, Jerusalem 1897, there f. 30b ff.; also the document from 1757 according to a copy he had found in Bukhara! <note>Novelistic adaptation of records by a Chelm Jew, Schaje Tripolsky, concerning the <term>Golem</term> legends circulating in Chelm. This adaptation renders the main part of the book useless. What can be discerned appears to be quite recent. In Chelm, they have even forgotten that the <term>Golem</term> is, by Kabbalistic necessity, mute. Only specific details remain noteworthy.</note>

192 --- *Der Prager Golem von seiner Geburt [!] bis zu seinem Tod* [The Prague <term>Golem</term> from its Birth [!] to its Death]. Adapted from an old manuscript [??]. With a foreword by Hans Ludwig Held.
[1st Edition] Vienna, Verlag v. Dr. Blochs Wochenschrift, 1919. 8°.
[2nd Edition] Berlin, Harz, 1920. 231 p. 8°.

<note>Translation of the—as Bloch persistently fails to mention—printed **נפ' אות מהר"ל** (*Nif’ot Maharal*, Piotrków 1909), a forgery from the 1890s that is as impudent as it is interesting. The forgery is blatant (see Eckstein **ס' יצירה**, below in the supplement, and Scholem) and owes its existence to apologetics against the latest iterations of the blood ritual mania. A list of—worthless—reviews of the book appears in the foreword to the 2nd edition. A portion of the stories had previously appeared in 1918/19 in Dr. Bloch’s “Wochenschrift.”</note>

193 --- **קבץ מכתבים מקוריים מהבעש"ט ז"ל ותלמידיו, על פי העתקות נאמנות ומדויקות, עם הערות ותמונות . . . נצרף לזה א) המשא ומתן בין לשכת חצר הקיסר בווינא עם נשיאות המדינה בלבוב, בענין האדמו"ר רבי ישראל מרוזין ז"ל אחר בריחו מרוסיא ולאוסטריא. ב) מכתב מקורי מהגאון . . מהר"ל מפראג משנת שמ"ג עם פקסימיליה, ע"ד יצירת הגולם.** [Collection of original letters from the <term>Baalshem</term> of blessed memory and his disciples, based on faithful and accurate copies, with notes and images... To this is added a) The negotiations between the office of the Imperial Court in Vienna and the state presidency in Lemberg, regarding the Admor <term>Rabbi Israel of Ruzhin</term> of blessed memory after his flight from Russia to Austria. b) An original letter from the Gaon... <term>Maharal of Prague</term> from the year 1583 with a facsimile, concerning the creation of the <term>Golem</term>.] Berlin-Vienna, Menorah Publishing, 1924. 111 p. 8°.

<note>“Collection of original letters of the <term>Baalshem</term> and his disciples, based on faithful and accurate copies, with notes and images, along with two appendices: a) official correspondence between Vienna and Lemberg regarding R. <note>Concerns a writing against Rabbi Joseph Ashkenazi—who later became famous in Safed—and his father-in-law Aaron, the Rabbi of Posen. Regarding the "festive occasion" on p. 3, at which the Chief Rabbi supposedly announced the "bold thought of the [recently occurred] death of <term>Asmodeus</term>," Bloch intended [verbally] that Purim be understood. In fact, however, the thought is not a joke, but is already presupposed in an old fragment in *Shushan Sodot* 1788 f. 55 a.</note>

336 **EMDEN, Jacob.** מטפחת ספרים. [*Mitpachath Sefarim* / The Veil of Books]. ... Part one and part two. Altona, at the house of the author, 528 [1768]. 50 leaves; 4°.
[Second Edition:] ... and now ... joined with it is the book *Ittur Sefarim* by Reuben Cohen Rapoport of Tarnopol, replying ... to the words of the author ... and also the biography of the author ... Lemberg, Michael Wolf, 632 [1872]. [12], 120 pp.; 8°.
“Mitpachath Sefarim...” A critique of the Zohar and an attempt to prove the late origin of large parts of it; cf. Graetz VII, Note 12. Still very valuable. “Torath ha-Kena’oth,” a history of Sabbatai Zevi and the Sabbatian sects and mystical heresies up to his time. The first work on Sabbatianism, and still very valuable.

“Sefath emeth...”, a communication and explanation of the amulets whose heretical content was attributed to Rabbi Jonathan Eibeschütz, published by Joseph Präger, a student of Emden. Important for the history of practical Kabbalah. The reprint also contains the book התאבקות [*Hitabkut*] immediately following it.*]

668 [**KNORR VON ROSENROTH, Christian.**] *Kabbala Denudata* [Kabbalah Unveiled], or the Transcendental, Metaphysical, and Theological Doctrine of the Hebrews. A work filled with various examples of the most ancient foreign philosophy, in which, before the translation of the Book of the **Sohar**, an Apparatus is provided. The first part of this Apparatus contains Kabbalistic Commonplaces, arranged in alphabetical order, which can serve as a Kabbalistic Lexicon. This small work contains:
I. A key to the ancient Kabbalah: that is, an explanation... of the divine names and titles from the book *Pardes*.
II. The book *Sha'are Orah*, or the Gate of Light, presented in alphabetical order...
III. Recent Kabbalah... of Rabbi Isaac Luria the German, translated into Latin from a manuscript.
IV. An index of many Kabbalistic matters presented in the book *Zohar* itself.
V. A compendium of the Kabbalistic-Chemical book called *Esh Mezareph*, concerning the Philosopher’s Stone, etc.
The second part, however, consists of various treatises, both didactic and polemical... The titles of the following parts will be placed before their respective volumes; a Latin index has been added.
Volumes [I]-II. Sulzbach, printed by Abraham Lichtenthaler, 1677, 1678; Frankfurt [am Main], at the expense of Johann David Zunner; printed by Balthasar Christoph Wust the Elder, 1684. 4º.
[Before the main title is an allegorical copperplate engraving.]
[Vol. 1] Editor's Preface; Latin Index of Materials of the First Part; Index of Passages of Holy Scripture from the Old Testament (17 unnumbered leaves).
Apparatus for the Book of *Zohar*.
Part one: Kabbalistic Commonplaces [!], p. 1—740.
[p. 33—36 skipped!]
Part two: 1. Excerpts from the Letter... regarding the utility of the translation of the Book of *Zohar*. 2. Kabbalistic Tables... 3—6. See under Henry More, Nos. 834—835. 7. Treatise on the Soul by Rabbi Moshe Cordovero. 8. ... Compendium of the book *Emek ham-Melech*. 9—11. See under Henry More, Nos. 836—839, p. 1—312.
[With only an intermediate title.]
Part three [with a detailed separate title for parts three and four, which are paginated continuously.] Sulzbach 1678. [Contains:]

<header>PAULY — PERINGER</header>

899 **PAULY**, Jean de. *Sepher ha-Zohar* <The Book of Splendor>.
Esoteric doctrine of the Israelites. Translated for the first time from the Chaldaic text and accompanied by notes. A posthumous work entirely revised, corrected, and completed. Published under the care of Émile Lafuma-Giraud.
I—VI. Paris, Leroux, 1906—1912. 8º.
I: 7 leaves, 557, [1] p. 2 plates. 1906.
II: 5 leaves, 741, [1] p. 1907.
III: 7 leaves, 492, [1] p. 1908.
IV: 3 leaves, 321, [1] p. 1909.
V: 3 leaves, 610, [1] p. 1909.
VI, 1: 3 leaves, 131, [1] p., 4 leaves 1911.
VI, 2: 2 leaves, 462 p., 4 leaves <note>Notes</note> 1911.

<note>Printed in 850 copies on paper with a special watermark. The numerous praising reviews are misleading; cf. Eisler, No. 327; M. Schwab, No. 1057; H. Hyvernat in *Revue Biblique*, new series 5 (1908), pp. 588—592; F. Martin in *Bulletin critique* 29, pp. 377—379. The translation, as it stands, is a compromise between de Pauly’s completely unusable translation, which reeks of ignorance, and a revision by an anonymous "competent scholar" (Back? cf. *Journal Asiatique* 10th Series, Vol. IX, p. 359), who also did not work particularly well. The notes are mostly based on direct forgeries and references to invented writings pulled out of thin air. The identity of de Pauly remains to be established. According to Joseph Halévy, *Revue Sémitique* 15, pp. 260—261, he was a zealous missionary who worked toward the conversion of the . . . <term>Hassidim</term>. Paulus Meyer, the notorious renegade, also appeared as Pawly (Jos. Bloch’s *Memoirs*, Vienna 1920, p. 23, 8vo. de Pauly's first Judaic work was a German translation of the *Shulchan Aruch*). The Zohar translation was made in the years 1900 to the end of 1903 at the request of Lafuma; cf. also Vulliaud, No. 1161, Vol. II, pp. 261—262 regarding his person. An anthology is:</note>

900 — *Le Livre du Zohar* (The Book of the Zohar). Pages translated from the Chaldaic. Paris, F. Rieder, 1925. 282, [2] p. 8º.
<note>= Judaism; Works published under the direction of Edmond Fleg, Vol. II.</note>
<note>The style of the large edition is occasionally improved. Foreword by E. Fleg. The selection is quite good.</note>

901 **PERINGER**, Georg. *De amuletis Hebraeorum disputatio* (A disputation on the amulets of the Hebrews), respondent L. J. Weslander. Helmstedt 1685. 8º.
<note>Almanzi Catalog, No. 4323 "very rare." According to Wolf II, 1214 "7 sheets," but listed there as an Uppsala dissertation, and the author's first name is given as Gustav.</note>

1179 **WERNSDORF**, Gottlieb. *Gründlicher Erweiß, daß Herr Dr. I. F. Buddeus in seiner so genannten Abfertigung der unbefugten Beschuldigungen den von ihm wegen der Cabbalae entstandenen Verdacht nicht abgelehnet, sondern vielmehr mit anstößigen Lehren gehäuffet, auf der alten reinen Theologorum Beyfall sich fälschlich berufen . . .* [Thorough proof that Dr. J. F. Buddeus, in his so-called "Dismissal of Unauthorized Accusations," has not refuted the suspicion raised against him regarding the Kabbalah, but rather increased it with offensive doctrines, while falsely claiming the approval of the old, pure theologians . . .] Wittenberg, Chr. <note>With a preface by the corrector Immanuel ben Gabriel from Coropoli (?) “of the Galliko family.” Following this: “Decision of the Gaon R. Isaac de Lattes,” who permits the printing of the Zohar. <page-num>167</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX</header>

The text in all printings, except for numbers 2, 3, and 4, is arranged according to this edition. C. B. 3477; Roest 1070; Wiener 3384. Catalog Schwager & Fränkel 26, No. 60, lists a copy “with very wide margins.” A parchment printing of this edition (also with wide margins and in very fine condition) is located in the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris and in the possession of the Feuchtwanger family in Munich; see Freimann in *Z. f. H. B.* XV, p. 83.

### 2 Cremona, Vicenzo Conti, 5319—5320 [1559—1560]. 2º.

Genesis: 132 leaves; Exodus: 122 leaves; Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy: 146 leaves.

<note>The title page shows these years: begun 5319, concluded 5320. In the colophon, however, the date for the completion of the entire printing is Friday, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5319 (December 1558)! The subsequent censorship permission from Father Galeaz Guacius is dated Cremona, August 5, 1558. The printing would therefore be roughly contemporary with the previous one. However, the editors' preface already argues against the sins of omission in the Mantua edition, the third part of which they already know. At the end of the preface are verses by the correctors: Chajim ben Samuel ibn Gatigno and Vittorio Aliano (the baptized grandson of the grammarian Elia Levita). The main part is in square script, and the additions are in Rashi script. At the beginning of each of the five main parts are large, decorated initials. In a few places, there are white gaps due to censorship. The text deviates in many ways from edition 1, both in arrangement and content. The individual readings are not always better than those in edition 1. The promised register of Bible passages is missing here as well! The Zohar manuscript Munich Cod. hebr. 203, written by Chajim ibn Gatigno in 1551, was not used for the printing and differs from it in many details. C. B. 3478; Roest p. 1071; Wiener 3385. Jellinek in his Kontres ha-Mafte’ach (1881), p. 8.</note>

### 3 Lublin, Zwi ben Abraham Kalonymus Jaffe, 5383—5384 [1623—1624].

132, 122, 146 leaves. 2º.

<note>Preface is the same as in the Cremona edition, but without the poem; in its place is a preliminary remark by Nathan ben Isaac Shapira. Decorated initials appear at the beginning of the main sections. The printing follows edition 2 word for row, but with corruptions and numerous printing errors. Colophon: finished Friday, the 18th of Tammuz 5384. C. B. 3479; Roest 1071; Wiener 3386 A.</note>

### — Venice???

<note>According to the preface of his *Imre Binah*, R. Isachar Bär ben Petachja (Prague 1611) claimed to have seen a Venice edition of the Zohar. A confusion with the Mantua edition seems likely. In Venice, only the *Midrash Ruth ha-ne'elam* had been printed in 1566 (see below). See also *Rav Pe'alim*, edited by Chones, p. 57.</note>

### — Amsterdam, 5430 [1670]

This is listed in the catalog of the Michael Library (1848) as No. 1164—1166, as well as in the Ghirondi-Schönblum catalog, No. 317 (where the date מ"ה יעש"ה is an error for the 1715 edition, as the full date reads מ"ה יעש"ה אד"ם. See C. B. 3481 a!).

<summary>This page details the 16th and 17th-century editions of the Zohar printed in Cremona and Lublin, noting their textual variations, censorship, and editorial history. It also addresses potential bibliographic errors regarding rumored editions in Venice and Amsterdam.</summary>
<keywords>Cremona edition, Vicenzo Conti, Lublin edition, Zwi ben Abraham Kalonymus Jaffe, Rashi script, censorship gaps, Chajim ben Samuel ibn Gatigno, Vittorio Aliano, Nathan ben Isaac Shapira, Venice printing, Amsterdam printing errors</keywords>

## 4 Sulzbach, Mose ben Uri Schraga Bloch, 5444 [1684].
[6], 132, 110, 128, 16 leaves. 2°.

[This is a combination of the two reviews from Mantua and Cremona, based on the latter. However, it seems that some passages, some of them strange, have been newly inserted. (For example, leaf 28 b = volume I, 37 of the Mantua edition, contains a piece that blatantly contradicts Mishna Berakhoth III, 3!) The edition was commissioned by Knorr von Rosenroth. It contains, for the first time, the remarks by Vital and variants from the *Derekh 'Emeth*—which were repeated in subsequent editions—as well as the word explanations of Issachar Baer in *Imre Binah*. The index of biblical passages, *Petach 'Enayim*—see E1 below—by Eliezer Manes, is printed at the end of the work. It includes a Latin title page and a dedication page to Christian August, Count Palatine of Sulzbach, which has been removed from almost all copies originating from Jewish ownership! The text is in <term>square script</term>. It includes a preface by the printer and the ‘decision’ of Rabbi Isaac de Lattes.
C. B. 3480; Roest p. 1071; Wiener 3387 A; Weinberg in the *Yearbook of the Jewish-Literary Society* I, p. 33 and XV, p. 127.]

## 5 Amsterdam, Salomo Proops, 5475 [1715]. 3 Volumes. 8°.
Genesis: [8], 251, 11 leaves; Exod.: 269, [1], [1]; Levit.-Deuteron.: 299, [10] leaves.

[This edition is the first to include the additions <term>השמטות</term> <note>hashmatot, or omissions</note> of the Mantua review from the Cremona edition and the *Zohar Chadash* at the end of each volume, which were included in all editions from then on. At the end of the third volume is the real-index (brought from Palestine by A. Rovigo, printed here without naming him; see below in E!). Edited by Meshullam Phoebus ben Isaac Heilprin. C. B. 3481; Roest p. 1071; Wiener 3388 A.]

## 6 Amsterdam, Salomo Proops, 5488 [1728]. 8°.
I: [8], 251, 10 leaves; II: 269 leaves; III: 299, [1] leaves.

[According to the previous edition! Labeled as the “second” Amsterdam printing! C. B. 3482; Wiener 3389.]

## 7 Constantinople, Jona ben Jakob, 5496---5497 [1736]. 3 Volumes. 4°.
I: [6], 251, 18 leaves; II: 279, [1] leaves; 309 leaves.

[With a preface by the printer. The Mantua review was revised here based on several Zohar manuscripts from the circle of Isaac Luria's disciples, and it contains additions from a manuscript of Rabbi Israel Benjamin from this circle. The edition enjoyed the highest reputation in the circles of the Kabbalists and was considered authoritative. Zedner p. 705; Wiener 3390A (listed as 8°!); Seeligman: *Catalogue van Biema* (Amsterdam 1907), p. 40 No. 691.]

## 8 Frankfurt a. d. Oder, without a stated printer [Bezalel ben Loeb], 5500 to 5501 [1740—1741]. 3 Volumes. 8°.
I: [10], 251, 15 leaves; II: 269, [3] leaves; III: 299, [1], 14 leaves.

[Very poor printing and text. In several catalogs, the incorrect location Frankfurt a. M. <note>Frankfurt am Main</note> is found! Roest p. 1071; Wiener 3391 A.]

3 Venice, Gerolamo Bragadino, 5418 [1658].
[Part I;] 5418 [1658]. [2], 96 leaves. Quarto (4°).
[Part II;] 5418 [1658]. 58, 40 leaves. Quarto (4°).
<note>Edited by Josef Chamis and corrected by Moses Zacuto, with a short preface by the former. The date 1663 in many catalogs is based on an error in calculating the year on the title page of the first part. Part II is unmistakably dated נוצ"ר חס"ד = 418. The arrangement is somewhat changed. All subsequent printings follow this arrangement. Part II also contains the <term>Midrash Ruth</term> as well as <term>Tiqqunim</term> to the <term>Zohar Chadash</term>, which are now always printed with it. Part II contains folios 55–58, an index of the biblical verses explained in the <term>Midrash Hane’elam</term> for the Song of Solomon, Ruth, and Lamentations, which was not printed in later editions. Good printing. C. B. 3499; Wiener 3410 A.</note>

4 Amsterdam, Moses Mendes Cutinho [קוטייניו], 5462 [1702]. 89 leaves. Quarto (4°).
<note>Incorrectly paginated from folio 61 to the end.</note>
<note>Corrected by Isaac ben Abraham Neustadt. Contains all pieces united in one volume. Small type. At the end, for the first time, the פירוש המלות מזהר גדול ומוזהר חדש, a short <term>Zohar</term> lexicon (2 leaves) by Judah Leib, the son of the editor. C. B. 3500; Roest p. 1073; Wiener 3411.</note>

5 Constantinople, Jona ben Jakob, 5500 [1740]. 177 leaves. Quarto (4°).
<note>With a short preface. Following the two preceding editions. At the end, from a manuscript, the book <term>Sefer Sod Hashem</term> regarding the ten <term>Sefirot</term>, as well as an explanation of difficult words.</note>

6 Korzec, ["Koretz"], Johann Anton Krüger, 5644 [1784]. [1] 123 leaves. Quarto (4°).
<note>Based on the Amsterdam edition. With the explanation of words.</note>

# E) Commentaries and Explanatory Writings on the Zohar.

<note>Writings by Kabbalistic authors that are not specifically dedicated to the Zohar (in its entirety or in individual parts) but which explain Zohar passages during the development of a Kabbalistic system are not included here. In a broader sense, almost the entire later Kabbalistic literature could otherwise be classified under this category.</note>

1 [ANONYMOUS:] ס' יודע יצחק <term>Sefer Yodea Yitzchak</term>.
Index to the <term>Zohar</term> and a treatise on the 7 <term>Hechaloth</term>.
[Krakow]. Without indication of the printer [Menachem Meisels], undated [between 1632—1648]. 4°.
<note>C. B. 3475. Friedberg, History of Hebrew Typography in Krakow (1900), p. 26, gives the date as 1632.</note>

2 [ANONYMOUS:] מפתח הזוהר <term>Mafteach ha-Zohar</term>.
Alphabetical subject index to the <term>Zohar</term>, <term>Zohar Chadash</term>, and the <term>Tiqqunim</term>. Brought from Jerusalem by Abraham Rovigo. With a foreword and afterword by the editor and proofreader [Mose Chagis].
Amsterdam, Natanael Foa, 5470 [1710]. [1], 24 leaves. 8°.
<note>Printed as מפתח מזוherd גדול ומזוהר חדש ומתקונים (Index to the Great Zohar, New Zohar, and Tikunim), omitting the foreword and afterword; also included in many editions of the Zohar at the end of the third volume, often with its own pagination. First appeared in the Amsterdam edition of 1715. Almost all editions since 1840 include this index.</note>

— [ANONYMOUS:] תהלים עם פי' הזוהר הקדוש <term>Tehillim</term> (Psalms) with the Commentary of the Holy <term>Zohar</term>. See: Israel ben Mose.

3 **ABRAHAM ABELE** of Drohobycz: ס' באר אברהם <term>Sefer Beer Avraham</term>.
Commentary on the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, by a student of the Hasidic leader Jacob Isaac of Lublin, but without Hasidic influence. Edited by his grandson Jekutiel Zalman Leib Kohen.
Lemberg, Uri Wolf Salat, 5629/1868. [4], 56 leaves. 4°.

— **ABRAHAM BEN ELIA** of Vilna. See: Elia ben Salomo: תקוני הזוהר <term>Tikune ha-Zohar</term> (No. 31).

4 **AARON SELIG** ben Moses of Zolkiew: חבור עמודי שבע <term>Chibur Amudei Sheva</term>.
A philological compendium on the <term>Zohar</term>, in five parts, with a preface. Contains: 1. Brief remarks and word explanations (following the arrangement of the Lublin edition of 1623) drawn from the writings of Meir ben Gabbai, Cordovero, Judah Hayyat, Recanati, Elia de Vidas, and Sheftel Hurwitz, as well as—most importantly—from the handwritten marginal notes of Rabbi Menachem Tiktin in his own copy of the <term>Zohar</term>. 2. Passages of the <term>Zohar</term> from the Mantua edition that are missing from the Cremona edition. 3. An index of the <term>Zohar</term> passages explained by the six aforementioned authors. 4. The same for the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>. 5. A list of parallel passages in the <term>Zohar</term> containing different versions, treating 39 such pieces.
Krakow, Menachem Nachum ben Moses Meisels, 5395/5396 [1635]. 36 leaves. Folio (2°).
<note>Of extreme rarity. Only two copies appear to be known: one in the British Museum and one in the Jerusalem National Library, from the collection of van Biema.</note>

### 5 **ALEXANDER SÜSSKIND** [ben Mose] of Grodno: <note>18th Century</note> ס' קרני אור <term>Sefer Karnei Or</term>

Short commentary on the <term>Zohar</term> according to Lurianic principles. Edited with additions by Naftali Hirz ben Aryeh Leib Halevi, published by his grandson Mose Halevi.

Vilna, Romm, 5642/1882. [2], 83 leaves. 8º.
Vilna, Romm, 5673/1912. [2], 83 leaves. 8º. <note>Stereotype print.</note>

### 6 **ALFASSI, Mas'ud** and **SALLUM, Mose**: כתם אופיר <term>Kethem Ophir</term>

Commentary on the <term>Zohar</term>, in the form of short, mostly quite pilpulistic remarks. Printed in the <term>Zohar</term> edition of Jona Chay Ro'eh (Section A No. 48):

Livorno, Israel Costa and partners, 5632—5649 [1872—1889]. 4º.

### 7 **ANUSHINSKI, Schneur Zalman Dovber**: ס' מצב הישר <term>Sefer Matzav ha-Yashar</term>

Responsa on difficult passages in the non-mystical, exoteric parts of the <term>Zohar</term>, for the reconciliation of contradictions between the <term>Zohar</term> and the remaining source works of Halakhic and Midrashic literature, at the same time with apologetic regard for modern critics. The work, which shows extraordinary erudition, was highly esteemed by the rabbinical authorities of Poland and Russia and is indeed of high interest, although written in the spirit of <term>Pilpul</term>. Of the very extensive book, as far as I could determine, only two volumes on <term>Zohar Genesis</term> appeared in print, "as much as a drop from the sea," which together contain 29, mostly very detailed responsa. Most interesting is No. 20 (II, 66—82) regarding the authorship of the <term>Zohar</term>.

I: חלק ראשון מן ספר בראשית <term>Part One of the Book of Genesis</term>; Vilna, Abraham Zwi Katzenelenbogen, 5641/1881. [7], 40 leaves. 2º.
II: מהדורא תניינא, חלק שני מן ספר בראשית <term>Second Edition, Part Two of the Book of Genesis</term>; Vilna, the same typographer, 5647/1887. [1], 93 leaves. 2º.
<note>Volume I contains 11 folio pages of approbations!</note>

### 8 **AZULAI, Abraham ben Mordechai**: ס' אור החמה <term>Sefer Or ha-Chammah</term>

Detailed, valuable commentary, composed in Hebron from 1624 onward. Contains, distinct from one another, only excerpts from the great manuscript commentaries of Moses Cordovero (אור היקר <term>Or ha-Yakar</term>) and Chayim Vital before his acquaintance with Isaac Luria, as well as from anonymous marginal notes in a <term>Zohar</term> copy of the Mantua edition. With a preface by the compiler, according to which this work was the second part of his great <term>Zohar</term> work *Kiryat Arba*. The 1st part: Or

Commentary on difficult passages of the Zohar, according to Lurianic principles, partly compiled literally from the writings of Chaim Vital.

*   **[1st Printing:]**

Finally, some halakhic responsa. Paginated with Hebrew characters up to and including f. 177, then 178–193 with Arabic numerals. However, the Hebrew pagination is followed by:

### 23 CHIZKUNI, Abraham: <term>ס' יד רמה וזיו ה'</term>

Double commentary on the <term>Zohar</term>. R. Shabbetai, the author of the old bibliographic work <term>Sifte Yeshenim</term>, saw folio-printed sheets of this work in Wilhermsdorf (which exists in manuscript in Oxford, Cod. Oppenheim 963). Are any pieces traceable?

### 24 CRISPIN, Isaac ben Menachem: <term>זהורי חמה</term>

A compilation of all passages relating to the five <term>Megilloth</term> from the <term>Zohar</term>, <term>Zohar Chadash</term>, and <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, arranged according to the sequence of biblical verses. At the end are 2 leaves of Judeo-Spanish poetry.

Salonika, Moses ben Samuel Falcon, 5498 [1738]. [2], 112, [2] leaves. 4°.

<note>The same, specifically regarding the Book of Esther:</note>

Lemberg, U. W. Salat, published by I. M. Nik, 5625 [1865]. [8] unpaginated leaves. 4°.

### 25 DAVID ben Abraham Shemarja: <term>ס' תורת אמת</term>

Excerpts from the <term>Zohar</term> with detailed word and subject explanations, which appear separately under the text as <term>דוד הקטן</term>. With an interesting preface. The commentary cites many contemporary authorities. At the end is an index. Only the volume on Genesis was published. Exodus, etc., were intended to follow.

Salonika, Moses ben Samuel di Medina, 5364—5365 [1604—1605]. 264 leaves. 4°.

<note>Printing began: 14 Shevat 5364; Printing completed: 1 Iyar 5365.</note>

**DAVID ben Mose de Medina.** See: de Medina, David.

**DOW BÄR ben Shneur Zalman.** See: Shneur Zalman ben Baruch.

However, the printed portion contains only remarks on <term>Zohar</term> III, 151a to 170b.

Vilna, Menachem Man ben Baruch, 5570 [1810]. [44] unnumbered leaves. 8°.

### 37 **FONTANELLA**, Israel Berachja ben Josef: <term>מפתחות הזהר</term>
**Part I:** Subject index to the Zohar, written around 1570 by an otherwise unknown Kabbalist named Samuel. Revised and edited by Israel Berachja Fontanella, with prefaces by the editor and the author, as well as approvals for the entire work.
**Part II:** Index of biblical passages cited in the Zohar, written by Fontanella. The best relevant index.
Venice, Bragadino, 5504 [1744]. 2 parts. 4°.
I: [4], 43, [1] leaves. II: [50] unnumbered leaves.

### 38 **GAǦ**, Josef: <term>זר זהב</term>
Commentary on the Zohar, in the form of continuous short remarks. Written in a pilpulistic style.
In the Zohar edition A 48: Livorno, Israel Costa, 1872—1889. 4°.
**GALANTE**, Abraham: <term>ירח יקר</term> see: **Azulaj**, Abraham: <term>זהרי חמה</term>.

### 39 **GALANTE**, Mose ben Mordechaj: <term>מפתח הזוהר</term>
Index of the biblical passages cited in the Zohar (very incomplete!), followed by a short subject index as well as some unpublished Zohar passages. With a short preface. Column title: <term>מפתחות ספר הזוהר</term>.
Venice, without printer's name, 5626 [1566]. "33" leaves. 4°.
<note>In fact, 34 leaves, as leaves 33 and 34 are merely signed in reverse.</note>

### 40 **GELERNTER**, Mose ben Israel: <term>ס' תהלים עם פירוש הזוהר השלם</term>
An excellent complete compilation of all Zohar passages regarding the Psalms, arranged as a commentary on them. Includes the text, the commentary of Rashi, and a preface.
Petrikau [Piotrków], Natan Kronenberg, *printed by* Sh. Chenchinski, 5665/1905. 8, 432 pp. 8°.

### 41 **GIǦ**, Chalfa ben Elia: <term>כג"ן הירק</term>
A detailed commentary on the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, according to the writings of Vital, together with the (vocalized) text and extensive indexes. <note>Cf. above C No. 65.</note>
Jerusalem, [Part 1:] S. Zuckermann, [Part 2:] J. N. Lewi, *s. a.* [1912?]. IV, 163 leaves; 220 leaves. 2°.

### 42 **HURWITZ**, Zwi Hirsch ben Josua Mose: <term>ס' אספקלריה המאירה</term>
Commentary on the entire Zohar, published with additions by Mordechaj Model from Schwabach; it does not make use of Lurianic Kabbalah and is often valuable. Based on the Zohar edition of Lublin, 1623/24.
Fürth, Isaac ben David <term>זצ"ל</term> <note>the memory of the righteous is a blessing</note> [Zirndorfer?], 5576 [1776]. 124 leaves. 2°.

### 43 **ISAAK EISIK ben Jekutiel Zalman** from Polotsk:
-><term>תיקוני זוהר . . . עם פירוש . . . באר יצחק</term><-
Commentary on the *Tiqqune Zohar*, including the text (the latter in square script). Based on Lurianic principles. With prefaces by the author and the proofreader, as well as a mystical poem by the latter.
Zolkiew, David ben Menachem Man, Chajim David ben Ahron halewi Segal and his cousin Seew Wolf ben Gerson Segal, grandson of Uri Phöbus, 5538 [1778]. [4], 194 leaves. 4°.

### 44 **ISACHAR ben Naftali Kohen** from Szczebrzescin: <term>ס' מראה כהן</term>
Subject index to the Zohar, based on the Cremona edition. At the end, there is also an index of biblical passages. With a preface.
Krakow, Isaak ben Ahron from Prossnitz, 5349 [1589]. [53] leaves. 4°.
Amsterdam, Uri Phöbus ben Ahron halewi, 5433 [1673]. 60 leaves. small 4°.
<note>Translated completely into Latin in Knorr von Rosenroth, *Kabbala Denudata*, Volume II, part one, pp. 1—150. Sulzbach 1684.</note>

### 45 **ISACHAR BÄR ben Mose Petachja** from Kremnitz: <term>ס' אמרי בינה</term>
Glossary of difficult words in the Zohar as well as explanations of concepts.
Prague, Mose ben Bezalel Kaz, 5371 [December 1610].
<note>Later, since the Sulzbach edition of 1684, printed alongside the text in almost all editions of the Zohar.</note>

### 46 — <term>ס' יש שכר</term>
An index, enumeration, and explanation of all religious laws of a halakhic nature mentioned or alluded to in the Zohar, arranged according to the divisions of the *Shulchan Arukh*. With a short preface.
Prague, Mose ben Bezalel Kaz, 5369 [1609]. 79 leaves. 4°.
Warsaw, Nathan Schriftgießer, 5642 [1882]. 56 leaves. 8°.

### 47 — <term>ס' מקור חכמה</term>
The exoteric explanations of the Zohar on the Pentateuch, arranged by Torah portions and presented in a Hebrew adaptation, partially with additional explanation.
Prague, Mose ben Bezalel Kaz, 1st of Kislev 5371 [1610] — 14th of Tevet 5371 [1611]. 40 [last part incorrectly paginated] leaves. 4°.
<note>Approvals at the end of the book! The references are based on the Cremona edition!</note>

### ISRAEL ben Mose: <term>ס' תמים יחדיו</term>

A collection (though very incomplete) of Zohar passages regarding the Psalms, arranged as a commentary. The author's long preface is only included in the first edition. 51 JAFFE, Israel ben Ahron: <term>ס' אור ישראל</term>
Part 1: Emanation theory and explanation of Zohar passages.
Part 2: <term>Halakhot</term> ... according to kabbalistic principles and explanation of Zohar passages. Not following the textual order of the Zohar, but arranged according to subject matter. Based on Lurianic principles.
Frankfurt on the Oder, Michel Gottschalk, 5662 [1702]. [1], 7, 187 leaves. Folio.
<note>The book was vehemently attacked and accused of Sabbateanism. Indeed, such passages are found, for example, on folio 13a. The author denied authorship of these passages in the justification pamphlet Tiph'ereth Jisra'el (Fürth 1774), published by his grandson, and declared them to be interpolations.</note>
JACOB Wilna and his son Jerucham. See: Wilna.

52 JESAJA Menachem Mendel, Schochet in Lodz: <term>ס' ילקוט הזהר</term>
Detailed subject index to the Zohar, Zohar Chadash, and the <term>Tiqqunim</term>, arranged by keywords, as well as an index of the parables and stories found therein. Often useful.
Piotrków [Pětrkov], Henoch ben Jesaja Wolf Fahlmann, 5672/1912. [2], 92 leaves. Octavo.

53 JOSEF ben Schraga: <term>ס' ישע יה</term>
Glossary of difficult words in the Zohar, edited and supplemented with additions by Jesaja ben Eliezer Chajim from Nice. The author lived in the second half of the 15th century. The glossary is meager; the explanations, as in all such glossaries, are mostly guesswork.
Venice, Giovanni Vendramin, 5397 [1637]. 10 leaves. Quarto.
<note>From leaf 7b onward, mystical collectanea concerning the Grace after Meals.</note>

54 JOSEF CHAJIM ben Elia: <term>תקוני זוהר . . . עם פירוש בניהו</term>
Commentary on the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, kept fairly short and simple. Accompanied by the (vocalized) text. The author is one of the most famous kabbalists of the recent era in the East.
Jerusalem, J. N. Levi, 5663 [1903]. 2 parts. Quarto.
I: [2], 142 leaves; II: [1], 129 leaves (cf. C 62).

55 JUDA ben Salomo ha-kohen: <term>ס' אשמורת הבקר</term>
Extensive commentary on the Zohar up to II, 43, based on Lurianic teachings. Preceding each <term>Sidra</term> are the relevant passages from the <term>Sha'ar Ma'amarei Rashbi</term> by Ch. Vital (see below No. 88). Edited after the author's death by Mose ben Abraham de Castro.
Thessaloniki, Isaac Jakon, 5612 [1852]. [2], 418 leaves. Folio.

56 LABI, Simon: <term>ס' כתם פז</term>
A detailed commentary on the Zohar for Genesis (he also composed one for Exodus, but it remains unpublished), written without the use of the teachings originating from Safed. The author wrote in Tripoli in North Africa around 1550. The Zohar was, in part, not yet available to him in printed form. The commentary is often valuable. At the end, several poems by the author are printed.
Livorno, Eliezer Sa'dun, 5555 [1795]. 2 volumes. Quarto.
I: [2], 1—280 leaves; II [with a title page, but paginated continuously]: [2], 281—448 leaves.

57 — <term>באור (מקצת) מלות זרות שבספר הזוהר</term>
A short glossary of the difficult words in the Zohar. [First printed in *Yad ne'eman* by Rabbi Abraham Miranda:]
Salonika, without a printer's name, 5564 [1804]. leaves 63–64. (Folio).
[Subsequently reprinted from there in the collective work *Kebhuzath chakhamim* edited by W. Warnheim.]
Vienna, Ad. della Torre, 1861. pp. 82—87. (Octavo).

58 LAWUT, Abraham David: <term>ס' בית אהרן והוספת</term>
An index of the Bible passages cited in the major works of Talmudic, Midrashic, and Kabbalistic literature, including the Zohar, Zohar Chadash, and the <term>Tiqqunim</term> (the latter two are indexed only in this book!). Very useful.
Vilna, Juda Leib Maz, 5641/1880. [2], 179 leaves. Folio.

LEITMERITZ, Benjamin Wolf. See: Benjamin Wolf ben Isaak.

59 LONZANO, Menachem de: <term>ס' עמר מן</term>
A commentary on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>; relatively the most useful commentary. Published together with the text of the J. Z. by Samuel Luria. Large portions are also already contained in the polemic *Ben David* by Naftali ben David (see below, No. 72).
Vilna, Widow and Brothers Romm, 5642/1882. [1], 19 leaves. Octavo.
Vilna, same publisher, 5673/1912. [Stereotyped printing of the former.]

60 LURJA, David: <term>ס' נפש דוד</term>
Short remarks on the Zohar. Published as an appendix to *Jahel Or* by the Vilna Gaon (see above, No. 32), with separate pagination. Caption title.
Vilna, [Widow and Brothers Romm], (1882). 14 leaves. Octavo.
Vilna, [same publisher], (1912). [Stereotyped printing of the former.]

61 LURIA, David: <term>ויאסף דוד</term>
A glossary of the difficult words in the Zohar. Excerpted from a larger work by the author by the editor Samuel Luria.
As an appendix to the second edition of the author's <term>מאמר קדמות ספר הזוהר</term>: <note>Treatise on the Antiquity of the Book of the Zohar</note>
Warsaw, Meir Jechiel Halter, 5647/1887. p. 73—82. (8°.)
LURIA, Isaac. See: Vital, Chayim.

62 LUZZATTO, Moses Chayim: <term>ס' אדיר במרום</term>
A very detailed commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term>, based on Lurianic principles. Written around 1740. Edited by Samuel Luria.
Warsaw, Isaac Goldman, 5640/1880. 212, [4] p. 8°.

63 MAHARIL, Aaron Solomon: <term>בירורי המדות</term>
An anthology of the ethical and moralizing passages of the Zohar, arranged alphabetically by subject, with explanations and references to Talmudic parallels. At the end are explanations of Talmudic <term>Aggadoth</term>.
Jerusalem, Rohald Brothers, s. a. [1923]. 86 p. 8°.
<note>Of this work, up to page 66 concerns the Zohar.</note>

64 MARAGI, Jacob: <term>פירוש על האידרא זוטא קדישא</term>
A commentary on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>, based on Lurianic principles. The underlying text shows variants from the printed text of the Idra. Written around 1700 in Morocco. The actual name of the commentary (in manuscripts) is <term>Imre Shepher</term>; the name of the (unpublished) commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term> is <term>Emeth le-Jakob</term> (Hirschfeld, Mss. of the Montefiore Library No. 345).
Vienna, Josef Schlesinger, 5647 [1887]. 40 leaves. 8°.
MARGOLIOUTH, Gerson: <term>אורי זוהר</term>. See: Israel ben Moses: <term>תמים יחדיו</term>.

65 DE MEDINA, David ben Moses: <term>ס' רוח דוד</term>
A commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term>, based on Lurianic principles. Written in Jerusalem. Includes a preface and a mystical poem in honor of Simeon ben Jochai with the author's own commentary. The second part, titled <term>Nishmath David</term>, contains a commentary on the Song of Songs written according to the same principles.
Salonica, Bezalel Halevi Ashkenazi, 5507 [1747]. [3], 79 leaves. 4°.
<note>Concerning the Zohar up to leaf 50.</note>

### 66 MEÏR ben Moses of Kornik: <term>ס' הררי קודש</term>

Commentary on the first and last <term>Mishnah</term> of the <term>Book of Yetzirah</term>, and on the <term>Zohar</term> passages that are recited on the nights of <term>Shavuot</term> and <term>Hoshana Rabbah</term>.

Dyhernfurth, Josef Mai, 5572 [1812]. 16 leaves. 8°.

### 67 MENACHEM AZARIAH [ben Isaac Berachiah] of Fano: <term>מאמר שברי לוחות</term>

An explanation of contradictory and striking passages in the <term>Zohar</term>, specifically in the <term>Ra'aya Mehemna</term>. With a foreword by R. Samuel Heller in Safed and a sermon by R. Solomon Alkabez.

Safed, Dow Bär ben Samuel Karo, 5624 [1864]. [1], 20 leaves. 4°.

MENACHEM de Lonzano. See: Lonzano, Menachem.

### 68 MENACHEM MENDEL of Lublin: <term>ס' תמים יחדיו</term>

An index, and in part a brief citation of all <term>Pentateuch</term> passages quoted in the <term>Zohar</term>. Heavily revised and published after the author's death with a foreword by Abraham ben Elijah of Vilna. Quite valuable.

Vilna, Typography of the priest Ludański, 5568 [1808]. [4], 68 leaves. small 4°.

<note>Leaves 25 and 26 were skipped in the numbering.</note>

### 69 MENACHEM MENDEL of Shklow: <term>ס' מים אדירים</term>

A very detailed commentary on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>, with additions and explanations by his student Isaac Eisik Chaver [Wildmann], under the name <term>Be'er Yitzchak</term>. In the style of M. Ch. Luzzatto's commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term>. Edited by Samuel Luria.

Warsaw, Isaac Goldman, 5646/1886. [1], 90 leaves. 8°.

### 70 MENACHEM MENDEL [ben Moses] of Vitebsk: <term>ס' מנחם ציון</term>

Commentary on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>. Composed around 1780 in Palestine. Published from a manuscript in the estate of R. Chayim Halberstamm in Neu-Sandez by Ze'ev Dov Heller. The very detailed commentary tends toward Hasidic homiletics.

Przemyśl, Żupnik, Knoller and Hamerschmidt, 1885. [2], 72 leaves. 4°.

<note>Under the same title, the author’s mystical commentary on the Book of Ruth was also printed in the same year and place.</note>

### 72 [**NAFTALI BEN DAVID**:] <term>ס' בן דוד</term>
    A polemical work against the commentary <term>Omer Man</term> by Menachem de Lonzano on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>, which at that time circulated only in manuscript. It follows this work line by line from the standpoint of the Lurianic system, which Lonzano allegedly did not treat with enough reverence. According to the preface, only 100 copies of the book were printed. The author's name is known from contemporary writings, as also hinted at in the preface. (Cf. Wiener 3690 regarding <term>וידע בירך</term>!)
    Amsterdam, without mention of the printer, 5489 [1729]. [10], 45 leaves. 8°.

**PALAĞI.** See: Falaği.

### 73 **PETAJA** (פתייא), **Joshua Mose Jecheskiel**: <term>יין הרקח</term>
    Commentary on both <term>Idras</term>, compiled from the <term>Shemonah She'arim</term> of Ch. Vital as well as the better-known Lurianic commentaries. Written for the <term>Idra Rabba</term> in collaboration with his father Mose in Baghdad 1884–1891; the commentary on the <term>Idra Zutta</term> in Jerusalem 1905–1908.
    Baghdad, Ezra Ruben Dangore, 5669 [1909]. 2 volumes. 8°.
    I (Idra Rabba): [8], 172 leaves; II (Idra Zutta): 100 leaves.
    [At the end, leaves 96–100, poems by his father.]

### 74 **PRILUK, Arje Leib**: <term>פירושי מאמרי זהר</term>
    Brief remarks on the <term>Zohar</term> from <term>Exodus</term> to <term>Leviticus</term>, section <term>Chukat</term>. Published from his estate by R. Juda Leib. Together with the <term>Midrash Konen</term> and the <term>Sefer Mussar</term> by the author.
    Berlin, Nathan Neumark, 5484 [1724], leaves 8–25. (8°).

### 75 **ROSENBERG, Juda ben Israel Isaac**: <term>ס' זהר תורה</term>. 5 volumes. 4°.
    Hebrew translation of large parts of the <term>Zohar</term>, rearranged according to the sections of the <term>Pentateuch</term>, with facing Hebrew and Aramaic text, "so that everyone may easily learn the Aramaic of the Zohar." All difficult and mystical passages are omitted. With commentary notes under the title <term>Ziv ha-Zohar</term> and a preface on Zohar translation in the first volume (<term>Genesis</term>), which appeared in the 1st edition under the title <term>Sha'arei Zohar Torah</term>. The book is a charlatanry.

### 78 **SAFRIN**, Eliezer Zwi ben Isaac Eisik Juda Jechiel: <term>ס' דמשק אליעזר</term>
Detailed commentary on the <term>Zohar</term> "on almost every word," in the sense of the Lurianic teachings and according to the manner of the Ziditchov school of Kabbalists. Begun in 1875. Edited by his son Isaac Moses Safrin in Komarno. It appeared only up to Exodus f. 269; the publication seems to have been suspended during the war. With an extensive preface.
Volume I: Przemyśl, Żupnik and Knoller, 5662/1902. [1], 126 leaves. 2°.
Volume II: Przemyśl, the same, 5664/1904. [2], 88 leaves. 2°.
Volume III: Przemyśl, the same, 5669/1908. [1], 91 leaves. 2°.

### 79 **SAFRIN**, Isaac Eisik Juda Jechiel [in Komarno]: <term>ס' זוhr חי</term>
A detailed commentary on the <term>Zohar</term>, according to the teachings of Luria and Hasidism; in the spirit of the teachings of his uncle and teacher Zwi Hirsch of Żydaczów. Composed from 1866 to 1873, when the author died. The commentary breaks off at the very beginning of Deuteronomy. Contains much Hasidic material. Edited by his son Eliezer Zwi Safrin (the author of No. 78!), with an extensive preface.
Volume I (Genesis): Lemberg, Abraham Nissan Süß and Jacob Meschullam Nik, 5635/1875. [4], 456, [1] leaves. 4°.
Volume II₁ (Exodus): Przemyśl, Żupnik and Knoller, 1878. [4], 166 leaves. 4°.
Volume II₂ (Exodus, with commentary on the <term>Sifra di-zeni'utha</term>): Przemyśl, Żupnik and Knoller, (1880). [2], 285, [1] leaves. 4°.
Volume III (Leviticus, Numbers, beginning of Deuteronomy): Przemyśl, Żupnik and Knoller, 1881. [2], 228, [5] leaves. 4°.

**SALLUM**, Moses. See: Alfassi, Mas'ud and Sallum, Moses: (No. 6).

### 81 **SALOMO** ben Juda ha-kohen: <term>ס' שעת רצון</term>
Commentary on the entire <term>Zohar</term> and the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term> according to Lurianic principles (excluding the <term>Zohar Chadash</term> and the <term>Idras</term>).
Salonika, Bezalel Halevi Ashkenazi, 5580 [1820]. 240 leaves. 2°.

### 82 — <term>ס' יפה שעה</term>
Commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term>, <term>Idra Zutta</term>, and the <term>Sifra de-Zeni'utha</term>, according to Lurianic principles.
Salonika, Josef Molcho, 5573 [1813]. [1], 167 leaves. 4°.
<note>Not identical with the commentary on Vital’s Ez Chajim published in Salonika under the same title! Bibliographies do not seem to know of this book at all.</note>

### 83 — <term>ס' הוראת שעה</term>
Kabbalistic treatises, particularly concerning the prayer book. Contains as its final section, leaves 63–78, a commentary on the "Zohar on the Song of Songs" in the <term>Zohar Chadash</term>. According to Lurianic principles.
Salonika, Bezalel Halevi Ashkenazi, 5578 [1818]. [1], 78 leaves. 2°.

**SAMUEL**. See: Fontanella, Israel Berachja: <term>מפתחות הזהר</term>

### 84 **SCHAPIRA**, Nathan ben Ruben: <term>ס' תורת נתן</term>
Explanatory commentary on passages of the <term>Zohar</term>, arranged in order. Published together with explanations by the author (Jerusalem, ca. 1650) of Lurianic writings; edited by Josef ben Salomo of Safed. (Extant more completely in manuscripts.)
Lemberg, Uri W. Salat, 5645/1884. 52 leaves. 4°.

### 85 **SCHAPIRO**, Zwi Elimelech [ben Pessach] (of Dynów): <term>ס' הגהות מהרצ"א</term>
Commentary marginal notes on the <term>Zohar</term> and the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, published from the author's personal copy with a preface by Abraham Arum of Przemyśl.
Przemyśl, Żupnik and Knoller, 1899. [2], 44 leaves. 8°.

### 86 **SCHAPIRO**, Zwi Hirsch ben Salomo (in Munkács): <term>באר לחי רואי</term>
A very detailed and significant commentary on the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, primarily following Lurianic principles. Unfinished: of the 70 <term>Tiqqunim</term>, 55 are provided with commentary. Volume 3 was published posthumously, featuring a preface by the author's son, Chajim El. Schapiro.
Vol. I: Munkács, Perlstein Brothers at Kahana and Fried, 5663 [1903]. [3], 299 leaves. 4°. [Up to <term>Tiqqun</term> 17.]

### 91 ? VILNA, Jacob [and his son] Jerucham: <term>פירוש לתקוני זהר</term>
Commentary on the <term>Tiqqune Zohar</term>, allegedly printed in the edition of the <term>Tiqqunim</term> edited by Jerucham (C 5); apparently produced in only a few copies alongside the edition containing only the text, or else destroyed. Constantinople, Jona ben Jacob, 1740.

### 92 ZACUTO, Moses ben Mordecai: <term>ס' יודעי בינה</term>
Commentary on the <term>Zohar</term>, according to Lurianic principles. Apparently, only the volume on Genesis was printed, of which Joseph Chamiz wrote up to leaf 33 (Zacuto in the afterword to No. 22). The book, of which no copy seems to have survived—which is very striking—is mentioned by the author in a letter from 1672 as being printed (<term>אגרות הרמ"ז</term>, Livorno 1780 f. 8 a), and Azulai still saw a piece of over 100 leaves. (The commentary is also preserved in manuscript; it appears several times in the Bodleian library).
[Venice, Bragadin, ca. 1663?]
Of the other parts, from Exodus to Deuteronomy, very large portions (perhaps all of them?) are printed under the (false?) name <term>ס' מקדש ה'</term>, specifically set apart, in the <term>Miqdash Melekh</term> of Shalom Buzaglo (No. 15).

### 94 ZEMACH, Jacob ben Chayim: <term>ס׳ זוהר הרקיע</term>
Commentary on many <term>Zohar</term> passages, arranged up to Leviticus. Edited from the records of Chayim Vital and provided with additions. Specifically contains detailed commentaries on the so-called <term>Sabha</term> in the section <term>Mishpatim</term> (II, 95—114) and on the <term>Sifra de-Tzeni'uta</term>. Regarding the latter, there is an additional anonymous detailed commentary by a student of Vital. Everything is according to Lurianic principles. Column titles first <term>פירוש הזוהר מהאר״י ז״ל</term>, then the intermediate title <term>ספרא דצניעותא</term>.
Korzec, ["Koretz"], Johann Anton Krüger, 5545 [1785]. [1], 178 leaves. 4°.
Marmaroś-Sziget, at the Marmaroscher Actien-Buchdruckerei, 5635/1875. [2], 204 leaves. 4°.
[Edited by Naftali Schönfeld.]

### 95 — <term>ס׳ קול ברמה</term>
Commentary on <term>Zohar</term> passages, from Numbers to Deuteronomy, as the second continuation of the work designated as the first part, <term>Zohar ha-Raqia</term>. However, it contains almost exclusively the extensive commentary on the <term>Idra Rabba</term> edited by J. Zemach, as well as the shorter one on the <term>Idra Zutta</term>. At the beginning, there are 32 rules for understanding the <term>Idra</term> according to the Lurianic interpretation. Written in 1643.
Korzec, Johann Anton Krüger, 5545 [1785]. [2], 1—107, II, 108 to 128 leaves. 4°.

### 96 ZLOTKI, Moses: <term>ס׳ נר משה</term>
The exoteric explanations of the <term>Zohar</term> for Genesis—Leviticus. With other mystical pieces.
Jerusalem, Isaac Gashzinni, 5642 [1882]. [3], 92 leaves. 8°.
ZWI ELIMELECH ben Pessach Schapiro. See: Schapiro, Zwi Elimelech.

<margin>99</margin>ZWI HIRSCH ben Jerachmiel Chotsch: **חמדת צבי**

A detailed commentary on the *Tiqqune Zohar*, according to Lurianic principles. Based on some reports about the author and the emblems on the title-page copperplate by El. Milsahagi (in **ראבי"ה** folio 27b, note 2) and others following him, it has been declared Sabbatian; however, this is difficult to substantiate from the content. It includes the text printed in square script and long introductory treatises. The main title is **ספר שבעים תקוני הזהר**.

Amsterdam, Moses ben Abraham Mendes Cutinho, 5466 [1706]. [8], 164 leaves. 2°.

<margin>100</margin>— **ס' נחלת צבי** [later printings: **נופת צופים**].

An anthology of the exoteric parts of the Zohar, especially the narrative and moralizing sections. In the Judeo-German [Yiddish] dialect. It was first translated by Abieser Seelig, an ancestor of the editor, and then revised by the editor and organized according to the sections of the Pentateuch. The book was very popular and was neither rare nor suppressed (as Bischoff claims in *Die Kabbala*, 1917, p. 75/76), but on the contrary, it was printed multiple times!

Frankfurt am Main, Anton Heinscheit, 5471 [1711]. 2°.

[Sub-title: "Teitsch-Zohar".]

Korzec [?], Josef Ze'ew ben Elia, 5572 [? 1812 ?]. 92 leaves. 4°.

# ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS

### 1224 [ANONYMOUS]. 
Report on the superstitious or, as the Jews call it, practical Cabbalistic books, as well as others horribly blaspheming Christ's . . . honor and all of Christianity, found with the rabbis of the Jewish community settled in the Princely Brandenburg-Ansbach lands who were with Hirsch Fränckel. Along with an attached . . . <term>Responsum</term>, through which this Jew was sentenced to life imprisonment.
Ansbach, 1713. [More than?] 19 leaves. Folio.
<note>According to Schudt (No. 1047), also printed in:</note> *Electa juris publica*, Vol. VI, part 4, p. 225 ff.

### 1225 — Hasidism, its essence and relationship to Rabbinism.
In: *Izraelita* III (1868), p. 193—194, 201—202, 217—219.
<note>“Der Chassidismus, sein Wesen und seine Verbindung mit dem Rabbinismus.”</note>

### 1226 [—]. 
The history of the great imposter or false Jewish King Sabbatai Zevi of Smyrna, who in the year 1666 set himself up as a King of the Jews in Turkey, but afterwards accepted the Mohammedan faith and died as a Turk in Constantinople in the year 1676. Printed 1702 (no place), 18 p. Folio, (with a portrait of Sabbatai Zevi before the title page, and “Sabbatai Zevi in prison” in the middle of the book).
<note>Whether this is identical to the “History of Sabbatai Zevi” allegedly printed in Frankfurt am Main, 1707, in folio (according to Grätz X, Note 3, § 1), which is taken from John Evelyn’s “History of the three impostors” — appearing in English and German in 1669 — cf. Fürst III, 186?</note>

### 1227 [—]. 
Letter in which it is briefly and concisely contained:
I. That everything which has been circulated regarding the new prophet Nathan Levi and the self-proclaimed King of the Jews is unfounded.
II. Nevertheless, the Jews have cause, given the nature of the matter, to be wary themselves and to be instructed from their own writings:
First, that the time of the promised Messiah has already passed.
Second, that everyone who, for 1600 years, has set himself up as the Messiah, has not only become a laughingstock and a disgrace to himself, but has also brought the entire Jewish nation to irreparable harm.

It includes details on specific editions, illustrations, and polemical letters refuting messianic claims.</summary>

## *SOURCES AND RESEARCH ON THE HISTORY OF JEWISH MYSTICISM*

->VOLUME II<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration set within an architectural frame consisting of two columns. - Second row: בינה (Binah) on the left, חכמה (Chokhmah) on the right

->P U B L I S H E D   B Y   W.   D R U G U L I N<-

<note>The Sephirotic Tree, or Tree of Life, is a central symbol in Kabbalah representing the ten attributes (Sephirot) through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals itself. The Hebrew terms correspond to: Keter (Crown), Binah (Understanding), Chokhmah (Wisdom), Gevurah (Strength/Severity), Gedulah (Greatness/Mercy), Tiferet (Beauty), Hod (Splendor), Netzach (Victory), Yesod (Foundation), and Malkuth (Kingdom).</note>
